tasks.task: Find a news article on BBC News about the impact of the recent tech industry layoffs on the global economy. Summarize the key points and the name of the author, and provide the date of publication.
tasks.answer: Article: 'The ripple effects of layoffs' (on-page headline: 'The toll of layoff anxiety'), BBC Worklife, https://www.bbc.com/worklife/article/20230203-stress-anxiety-global-layoffs. Author: Josie Cox. Published: 6 February 2023 (2023-02-06T21:08:49.000Z). Key points: (1) Workers worldwide are experiencing severe anxiety and dread about being next to lose their jobs as layoffs sweep across industries, especially tech, where companies cut more than 150,000 workers in 2022 according to tracking sites. (2) Experts say this layoff wave is notable for its scope and scale because it comes even as underlying economic fundamentals improve - unlike the Great Recession, when US unemployment peaked at 10% with ~15 million unemployed; today the US rate is around 3.5%. (3) The cuts clash with the employee-centric, wellbeing-focused leadership championed during the pandemic, creating cognitive dissonance and eroding trust among both laid-off and remaining employees. (4) Experts warn that continued waves of layoffs - or even the looming threat of them - could deteriorate organisational cultures, with grim ripple effects on employee engagement, productivity and the wider economy. (5) There is an immediate human toll: research shows being laid off increases the risk of a host of health conditions, and the uncertainty itself harms workers' wellbeing.

tasks.task: Find the latest article in the Green Living section on BBC News and provide a summary of its main points.
tasks.answer: The latest article in the BBC News Green Living section (https://www.bbc.com/future-planet/green-living) is 'The Himalayan village where you can see the cosmos', published 1 September 2025 (https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20250829-the-himalayan-village-where-you-can-see-the-cosmos). Main points: (1) Hanle, a remote village in the barren, Moon-like landscape of Ladakh in northern India, has some of the darkest skies on Earth, rating 'one' (the darkest) on the Bortle dark-sky scale with about 270 clear nights a year, so the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye. (2) Since the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve was founded in 2022 - spanning 1,074 sq km, six villages, a monastery and 10 stationary telescopes - astrotourism has flourished, with homestays and trained local astro guides running stargazing expeditions. (3) The village hosts the Indian Astronomical Observatory on Mount Digpa Ratsa Ri, home to one of the world's highest optical telescopes (the Himalayan Chandra Telescope) and MACE, the world's second-largest gamma-ray telescope. (4) Hanle's annual Star Party, held each September during the brief four-month accessible window, draws stargazers and astrophotographers from across India. (5) Rising tourism brings income but also light-pollution concerns: villagers switch off lights at dusk (no power after 23:00), use blackout curtains and warm bulbs, and the Indian Institute of Astrophysics is adding measures such as road delineators and plans to decentralise astrotourism across Ladakh. (6) Practical tips: visit June-September around the new Moon, fly Delhi to Leh and acclimatise, arrange permits in advance and book homestays early.

tasks.task: Find the most recent article on BBC News about archaeological discoveries and summarize the main findings and their significance.
tasks.answer: Found the most recent BBC News article on archaeological discoveries: 'Roman settlement dating back 2,000 years found under new-build estate' (published 2026-11-07, BBC Wales, https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6r7ydgl44z7o). Main findings: A 'very significant' Roman settlement, including a jewellery workshop, was discovered under a new-build housing estate in Mancot, Flintshire, north-east Wales, by Heneb (the trust for Welsh archaeology) during mining surveys. Dozens of artefacts were recovered - pottery, coins (one from emperor Commodus AD 177-192 and one of Constantine ~200 years later), brooches and lead moulds - making it one of the biggest Roman artefact collections in the county; the site possibly originated in the Iron Age and saw successive occupation. Significance: The find changes understanding of the area's history, showing local industry exploited rich metal resources to produce decorative brooches and commodities likely servicing the Roman city of Chester, with pottery suggesting trade as far as mainland Europe. It challenges the long-held idea of a poor relationship between Romans and the native population, and experts call it the beginning of what could be a long period of discoveries in north-east Wales. Artefacts will be conserved at the National Museum of Wales in Cardiff before public display, possibly at Mold Museum in 2027.
